## Conclusion and Perspectives {#sec-conclusion}

::: {.section-subtitle}
What is proved, what is computed, and the open problems
:::

In this article, we extended our preliminary work [[QS15](#ref-QS15)] by relaxing the
unrealistic assumptions. In particular, the results hold when the durations satisfy the
triangular inequality, as well as under the assumption of [[QS15](#ref-QS15)]. First, we
defined three types of MultiZenoTravel problem: the symmetric clique, the non-symmetric clique and
the general version.

The algorithm to identify and build Pareto optimal plans relies on a single proposition. Due to
the increasing complexity of these problems, we first proved the proposition for the symmetric
problem, where the lists of $2t - p$ cities that can be flown, and how fast, are described by
admissible partitions and link forests. We then extended it to the non-symmetric version when no
flight between central cities is shorter than a detour through $C_I$ or $C_G$, the makespan of a
role configuration taking its waiting into account. Without this assumption, and for the general
version, we showed where the method stops: $B\bar A\bar B$ situations, and more generally patterns
with one flight between central cities, do not complete the Pareto front, and the reduction of a
general instance to a clique instance preserves it only in some cases, for which the exact front
is computed otherwise on small instances.

From an implementation point of view, we presented a version of the ZenoSolver whose running time
is pseudo-polynomial in the durations, although computing the makespan of a fixed list of cities
is strongly NP-hard. It returns each Pareto front with a certificate, which a checker verifies
without trusting the solver; the central theorems, a checker and a solver of their own are
formally verified in Lean 4. We demonstrated the diversity of Pareto-fronts which can be obtained
by changing the instance parameters, and gave the front of the default generator in closed form.
We validated the solver and the theory in a seeded experiment campaign against exhaustive
searches written independently of the solver. Finally, we provided a concrete application using
real-life data. Using the OpenFlights database, we used the ZenoSolver to find the Pareto-optimal
plans between the two largest airports in the world: exactly for three planes or more when the
planes fly only between these two airports and the intermediate ones, and within a bracket
otherwise.

Beside the direct interest for the route and schedule multi-objective optimization for air
transport, we believe that the work presented in this paper can be useful in many regards, and in
particular for the benchmarking and comparison of algorithms, and for exploratory landscape
analysis. Moreover, existing multi-objective planning instances are, as far as we know, not
offering the exact Pareto-front, which only allows the comparison between solvers but not to
characterize how hard is an instance and how far from an optimal solution the solvers are. On the
contrary, ZenoSolver is capable to return the Pareto Front, with at least one plan for each point
of the Pareto Front in the objective space.

Future work should focus on returning the entire Pareto set, i.e. all feasible plans for any
Pareto optimal objective vector. Another possible improvement would consist in characterizing the
*general* MultiZenoTravel instances for which the reduction to a *clique* MultiZenoTravel
preserves the Pareto front, and those for which it can be done in polynomial time.

### What is established {#sec-status}

The table summarises the status of the main results, from §0 of the
[theory note](https://github.com/aquemy/ZenoSolver/blob/master/doc/theory/exact-front.md). The
badge of each node says whether it is machine-checked; the [blueprint](../proofs.qmd) gives the
full status of every statement, and the [claim graph](../claimgraph.qmd) the history of each
claim.

| Setting | Pareto front characterized | Computed exactly |
|---|---|---|
| (S) and (A1) | by admissible partitions ({{< node "Theorem 4.7" badge=false >}}, {{< node "Corollary 4.8" badge=false >}}) | yes, pseudo-polynomial ({{< node "Corollary 8.3" badge=false >}}) |
| (S) and (AΔ) | by admissible partitions ({{< node "Theorem 4.10" badge=false >}}, {{< node "Corollary 4.12" badge=false >}}) | yes, pseudo-polynomial |
| (S) only | no, a plan can beat every admissible partition ({{< node "Example 4.13" badge=false >}}) | where the lower bound $L$ meets the plans found |
| Non-symmetric, (A1-NS) | by role configurations with least makespans ({{< node "Corollary 6.10" badge=false >}}) | bracket, then search over configurations |
| Non-symmetric, (AΔ) only | not by $B\bar A\bar B$ situations ({{< node "Proposition 6.7" badge=false >}}) nor by one central flight per pattern ({{< node "Proposition 6.18" badge=false >}}); open | small instances only (exhaustive search, flow model) |
| General graphs | the reduction is exact in three cases ({{< node "Proposition 6.15" badge=false >}}), not in general ({{< node "Example 6.11" badge=false >}}) | integer flows, level by level ({{< node "Proposition 6.16" badge=false >}}) |
| Linear family | closed form ({{< node "Theorem 10.1" badge=false >}}) | yes |

### Open problems {#sec-open}

1. **Symmetric instances without (A1) or (AΔ).** {{< node "Example 4.13" >}} shows that a plan can
   then beat every admissible partition. The relaxation $L$, and the admissible optimum computed
   with the shortest flight times $d'_x$ from each city to $C_I$ or $C_G$, remain lower bounds
   ({{< node "Lemma 3.4" >}}, {{< node "Theorem 4.10" >}}). The exact front is open.
2. **Non-symmetric instances with short central flights.** Neither $B\bar A\bar B$ situations
   nor patterns with one flight between central cities complete the front
   ({{< node "Proposition 6.7" >}}, {{< node "Proposition 6.18" >}}). Open: a combinatorial
   description of the front; whether some bound on the central landings of a pattern always
   suffices (the searches never needed more than six); and whether flights between central
   cities are useless whenever $d$ and $\bar d$ order the cities alike, as on all 150 instances
   searched. The claim of Proposition 6.18(d) about patterns $A$ rests on the flow model only and
   is a sketch.
3. **General graphs.** A characterization of the front in the spirit of
   {{< node "Corollary 6.10" >}}, with patterns that fly between central vertices from a $B$ to a
   $\bar B$, as in {{< node "Example 6.11" >}}, and costs charged by the paths actually flown; an
   exact algorithm faster than the integer flows of {{< node "Proposition 6.16" >}}; and the graph
   classes beyond {{< node "Proposition 6.15" >}} on which the reduction is exact. It fails on
   paths with two central vertices, hence on trees.
4. **Complexity.** Computing the makespan of a list is strongly NP-hard
   ({{< node "Theorem 8.1" >}}), but whether deciding $E(T) \le C$ is NP-hard, with $t$ written in
   unary as in PDDL, is not established.
5. **The greedy heuristic on the linear family.** {{< node "Conjecture 10.2" >}} states that it
   reaches the closed-form front; it holds on every instance tested so far. Offset progressions
   $d_i = a + bi$, on which $L < E$ occurs, have no closed form.
6. **PDDL semantics.** The correspondence between PDDL plans and the plans of this paper
   ({{< node "Statement 1.2" >}}) is argued but not formalised, and whether planners and the
   validator VAL accept zero-duration actions is not checked. Differential tests against VAL on
   the emitted plans would settle the practical side.
7. **Non-symmetric gaps.** {{< node "Theorem 6.9" >}} makes the search over role configurations
   exact; what remains is its cost, the number of configurations below the achieved cost at a gap,
   and the search over orders and matchings, which resembles non-preemptive open-shop scheduling.
8. **Formalisation.** The blueprint lists the statements whose proofs are written but not yet
   formalised in Lean, among which several results of the non-symmetric and general sections.
